explanation: Birds feel no burn from capsaicin, so they eat chillies and scatter the seeds unharmed, while mammals, whose teeth would crush the seeds, are put off.

claims.text: Capsaicin is the compound responsible for the heat of chilli peppers.
Piperine gives black pepper its bite, allicin forms in crushed garlic and menthol gives mint its cooling feel; none makes chillies hot.
Birds do not feel the burning sensation of capsaicin, because their version of the receptor it acts on is insensitive to it.
Birds eat chillies and pass the seeds intact, while mammals, which tend to crush seeds when chewing, are deterred by capsaicin.

evidence.restatement: Capsaicin is the compound that makes chilli peppers hot.
Piperine gives black pepper its bite, allicin forms when garlic is crushed and menthol gives mint its cooling feel.
Birds feel no burn from capsaicin because their version of the TRPV1 receptor is insensitive to it.
Birds swallow chilli seeds whole and pass them intact, spreading them, while seed-crushing mammals are deterred by the burn.
Capsaicin is the pungent compound of chillies and acts on the TRPV1 heat receptor.
Piperine is black pepper's bite, allicin forms when garlic is crushed, menthol triggers cold receptors; none is chilli heat.
Bird TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin (shown for chickens by Jordt and Julius, 2002), so birds do not feel the burn.
Directed deterrence: mammals chew and destroy seeds and avoid capsaicin, while birds swallow seeds whole and spread them (Tewksbury and Nabhan, 2001).
